title: Sen. Gillibrand says Democrats must end Iran war, hold Trump accountable. But how?
description:
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand on the Democratic Party's agenda for the next Congress 
    
        
                Download
body:
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand on the Democratic Party's agenda for the next Congress 
    
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6028837/nx-s1-9992793" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
        
    



      
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., attends a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing in Washington on April 30, 2026.
                
                    Graeme Sloan/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Graeme Sloan/Getty Images
    

   
   Democrats have won back Congress. Now comes the harder question: How much can they actually change with President Trump still in the White House?   "I dare him to veto that," Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York told Morning Edition, challenging Trump to reject bipartisan legislation restoring Medicaid coverage.   
   Gillibrand said Democrats would focus on lowering costs, restoring health care access and ending the war in Iran.   Democrats also face pressure to hold the Trump administration accountable, with new investigative powers and the possibility of a third impeachment.   Asked about impeachment, Gillibrand did not commit to pursuing it.   "We can do both," she said, proposing a ban on stock trading by members of Congress and senior administration officials.   
   Like other Democrats, Gillibrand cited the war in Iran as a factor in the party's election victories, saying Trump had broken his promise to avoid prolonged wars as the conflict drove up costs.   "We have to end this war in Iran," she said.   Trump acknowledged Wednesday that the war had contributed to Republicans' election losses. But the conflict continues, with Iranian officials warning against renewed U.S. attacks. How Democrats intend to bring the war to an end remains unclear.   In her interview with NPR's A Martínez, Gillibrand also discussed Democrats' gains in Republican states, Trump's ballroom and cuts to food assistance and medical research.   Listen to the full conversation by clicking the blue button above.    The digital version was edited by Treye Green.

title: What's the future of the Democratic party in Texas, amid historic midterm wins?
description: NPR's Ailsa Chang talks with former Texas state Sen. Wendy Davis, a Democrat, about Texas flipping blue and what it means for future elections.
body:
NPR's Ailsa Chang talks with former Texas state Sen. Wendy Davis, a Democrat, about Texas flipping blue and what it means for future elections.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AILSA CHANG, HOST:  OK. We're going to go now to somebody with a long history being in the minority when it comes to Texas politics. Democrat Wendy Davis, a former Texas state senator. Welcome.WENDY DAVIS: Thank you. I'm so happy to be on with you today.CHANG: So happy to have you. I want to start 12 years ago because you yourself ran for governor of Texas as a Democrat in 2014. You ran against Greg Abbott, and you lost by 20 points. And then this year, we see Democrat Gina Hinojosa also run against Greg Abbott. And she wins by this pretty comfortable margin, by about seven points. How surprised were you by that result?DAVIS: Surprised by the degree to which she won. But I've been part of Gina's team from the jump and was privileged to be seeing the data as we were looking at what was coming in on the early vote and testing that against the way the model had been built to determine, you know, whether Gina would be ahead.CHANG: Yeah.DAVIS: And we felt really good going into Election Day that she was positioned to win. And unless there had been some huge, unexpected turnout by Republicans that day, we felt like she was going to win. But the fact that she won by the margin that she won by.CHANG: Yeah.DAVIS: The fact that every statewide race underneath her was also one that a Democrat won, that we won state Supreme Court races, but also another very near and dear project to my heart, which has been to raise money for and invest in down ballot races. We flipped 21 state House seats last night.CHANG: And the question I have is, why do you think that was? I mean, we just heard my colleague, Ashley Lopez, talk a little bit about this. But what do you think changed between your run 12 years ago and today...DAVIS: Yeah.CHANG: ...To allow for such a different result against the same Republican candidate, at least in the governor's race, Greg Abbott?DAVIS: Yeah, I mean, if you go back to 2014, it was a year of tremendous complacency by Democrats, a similar complacency to what we saw from Republicans this cycle. And there's no question that this year was an absolute repudiation of Trump and his agenda, and the fact that Greg Abbott and other state leaders had absolutely traded what had been considered their prior more traditional conservative values for MAGA. And they had leaned so hard into that. But for Greg Abbott particularly, he had leaned very hard into the cruelty of the Trump immigration agenda. And he paid a price for that last night.CHANG: So it sounds like you - it sounds like what you're saying is last night, in Texas at least, it was more of a repudiation against Trump and Abbott and less about Democrats hitting on a different kind of message to Texans this time around?DAVIS: No. No, I don't want to leave that impression at all. The repudiation piece was part of it. But our Democrats offered something that I think was incredibly unique and pitch perfect. And I'll use Gina as the example of this. Gina knew from the outset what she wanted to deliver for the people of Texas. She gave, consistently throughout, a message of understanding the pain that they were feeling economically, really leaning into, in a very experienced and empathetic way, what was happening to their public schools and the loss of opportunity, the fact that so many people in our state don't have healthcare. And...CHANG: But if I may.DAVIS: Yes.CHANG: If I may, I want to talk about you and just...DAVIS: Yeah.CHANG: ...If you would like, to give you your flowers, because your name has been popping up a lot next to the name of Beto O'Rourke. As two Texas Democrats who tried to pave the way, do you feel like you helped build the momentum that we saw crest last night into this blue wave in Texas in about...DAVIS: I think...CHANG: ...Twenty seconds or so (laughter).DAVIS: I think every person that runs and, you know, raises resources and energizes voters helps to build the path for the people that come afterward. Beto did better than I did. And now Gina, of course, has crested that mountain. And I couldn't be more proud to have played a role in helping that along and staying involved. And that's what Beto did, too.CHANG: All right.DAVIS: Neither of us have given up on our state and we never will.CHANG: That is Democrat Wendy Davis, former Texas state Senator. Thank you.DAVIS: Thank you.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: The South flexes political power in midterms, sets regional influence in 2028 election
body:
Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks during an election night watch party on Nov. 3 in Atlanta. Bottoms will be the nation's first Black woman governor.
                
                    Megan Varner/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Megan Varner/Getty Images
    

   
   Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app      Tuesday's dramatic midterm results have transformed the electoral map, ensuring the future path to power for Democrats and Republicans alike must run through the South.   Black voter turnout surged in states like Louisiana and Georgia, as Democrats flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. Mississippi is too close to call.   Republican-led efforts to redraw House districts to gain more favorable districts in places like Alabama, North Carolina, Texas and Florida backfired, with Democrats poised to net several seats in the region.   
    Loading... 
   In several states, the margins at the top of the ticket were so large that the blue tsunami carried down ballot races along with it, flipping several state legislative chambers and statewide offices along the way.   Even in contests where Democrats ultimately did not prevail, the millions of dollars of investment from both sides and the wide-ranging repudiation of the Trump administration from every demographic group highlight the South's important role in control of Congress and the White House in future election cycles.   Redistricting   In the aftermath of a Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that gutted part of the Voting Rights Act, Republican-led Southern states rushed to redraw House maps to create additional seats that would better withstand a midterm environment where voters punished the party in power.   They included changes in Tennessee that split Memphis into three districts (and where Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson is within a few thousand votes of winning), a redraw of several Alabama districts that sought to unseat Rep. Shomari Figures (who won by nearly 8 points in the new Trump +14 configuration) and a target of nine seats in Texas and Florida.    Loading... 
   As of Wednesday night, Republicans have won one of them, according to a race call by the Associated Press.   Before Election Day, there were signs that the ruling, along with the war in Iran, rising costs, concerns about corruption with the Trump administration and other top issues would serve as a motivator for turnout among Black voters.    
   In primaries held after the ruling, Black voter participation soared. Ashley Kennedy Shelton with the Louisiana-based Power Coalition for Equity and Justice previously told NPR that the court decision was "personal" for Black voters.   "Everybody's spending more money on their electricity bills, their gas bills, their food bills," she said. "All of these different things are really personally impacting voters. And I think that for all the folks that used to say, 'I don't do politics!' I think they realize that politics is absolutely doing them, and they have to get involved."   In South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews flipped a U.S. Senate seat, the state saw record voting for a gubernatorial election year, driven in part by elevated Black turnout. It's a similar story in Louisiana, where Democrat Jamie Davis narrowly lost to Sen.-elect Julia Letlow by less than two percent in a state Trump won by more than 15 points in 2024.   
   Mississippi's Senate race is too close to call, with Democrat Scott Colom leading by less than 1200 votes against incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state with the highest share of Black voters in the country.   
   State level   It's not just Congress where the South is the center of shifting power. Big Democratic victories — or swings away from Republicans — at the top of the ticket led to an avalanche of shifting offices at the state and local level.   Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff's 18-point victory in Georgia helped propel former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms to victory in the governor's race, as Democrats swept every single statewide elected office, gained control of the state utility regulator and are set to win a majority in the state House.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                In this file photo from the 2026 election, people wait to vote in early voting for the midterm elections on Oct. 25 in Cary, N.C.
                
                    Allison Joyce/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Allison Joyce/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   In North Carolina, former Gov. Roy Cooper's 20-point victory was enough to potentially flip multiple congressional seats and win control of the state House.    Texas Democrats won a majority of seats in their state House, while Republican House supermajorities in Florida and South Carolina have ended, too. The down ballot gains extend into states that aren't as purple or blue, with dozens more pickups reported in Alabama, Arkansas, Kentucky and Tennessee.   2028 is now   The expansive majorities in the House and Senate built upon southern swings have implications far beyond the makeup of the next Congress, as both parties look ahead to the 2028 presidential election.     
   In the leadup to Election Day this year, potential presidential contenders from both parties have made varying efforts to offer financial support and campaign for nominees in tight races, including notable appearances by former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Georgia Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, chair of the Democratic Governors Association.   On the Republican side, Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and Vice President JD Vance are among those who focused on the region.   Even though Republicans held on to the Florida governor seat and U.S. Senate seat, closer-than-expected margins in statewide races and House races alike make the state an attractive investment for both parties seeking to gain an edge with voters for 2028, just like Democrats' romp in historically red Texas.   
   Together, Texas, Florida, Georgia and North Carolina represent more than a third of the 270 electoral votes needed to win the White House.

title: What's next for Democrats after the midterms. And, a look at the outstanding races
description: Democrats' First 100 Hours, Outstanding Midterm Races, Trump Doubles Down On Policies
body:
Democrats' First 100 Hours, Outstanding Midterm Races, Trump Doubles Down On Policies
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-152046/nx-s1-mx-6030264-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Democrats won this week in districts and states that President Trump carried by double digits just two years ago. The party now has its largest Senate majority since the passing of the Affordable Care Act during Obama's early presidency. Senate results from Alaska and Mississippi are still pending. If those races favor Democrats, their majority could grow to 54, plus the two independents who caucus with them.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The sun rises behind the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday.
                
                    Allison Robbert/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Allison Robbert/AP
    

   
   🎧 A few tight House races remain uncalled, but the swing toward Democrats already rivals the post-Nixon Watergate backlash, NPR's Tamara Keith tells Up First. She highlights two notable race surprises that happened this week. One was in Nevada's 2nd District, which has been Republican since the 1980s. Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson claimed victory overnight. The other was in Alabama's 2nd District, where Shomari Figures overcame redistricting that favored Trump by 14 points. Figures won by more than seven points.➡️ Mike Johnson plans to step down as top House Republican in the new Congress after a tough defeat for his party, according to a source familiar with his plans who was not authorized to discuss them publicly.➡️ Voters in 39 states, Washington, D.C., and the Northern Mariana Islands decided on 146 ballot measures covering issues like taxes, transgender rights, traffic cameras and data centers. Here's a summary of the results.   
   For more than a year, Democrats urged voters to elect them to lower costs and eliminate corruption. Now, the party must act to fulfill its campaign promise. The new Congress is unlikely to see much major legislation signed into law, but Democrats plan to launch ambitious investigations in the House and Senate. Democratic Party leaders and political analysts shared their insights with Morning Edition on the midterm election results, discussed the impacts of mid-decade redistricting efforts and outlined the party's next steps.   🎧 Most legislation still requires 60 votes to pass the Senate, and Trump has fluctuated between saying he will be Mr. Veto and expressing willingness to work with Democrats, NPR's Sam Gringlas says. Democrats are interested in restoring enhanced ACA health subsidies, reversing Medicaid cuts, asserting control over tariffs and pushing to end the war with Iran. Gringlas says this election has intensified pressure on Democrats. He points to a voter he met this summer, who said that if Democrats gained control, they would have to enact real changes, otherwise it wouldn't matter who they nominated for president in 2028.   Trump focused on his East Wing ballroom construction project during his first public appearance after the Republicans lost the House and Senate. When asked about the election, he said he wasn't to blame for his party's losses.   
   🎧 Trump quickly pointed out that he wasn't actually on the ballot, NPR's Emily Feng says. But he did urge voters to imagine he was. Voters associated his signature policies, like tariffs and the war in Iran, with rising inflation and gas prices. After Vice President JD Vance posted on social media yesterday suggesting that the war in Iran contributed to GOP losses, Trump somewhat agreed. The president cited its impact on pump prices, but doubled down on the war, saying he would act the same way again if he had to. With a Democratic Congress, Trump will encounter greater legislative gridlock, and Democrats could wield stricter funding controls on issues like immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict in Iran, Feng says.➡️ A new Democratic majority could pressure Trump to end the war in Iran. But directly influencing fuel prices, which are tied to the complex international oil market, will be challenging.   Life advice   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        Jan Hakan Dahlstrom/Getty Images/Stone RF
    

   
   Have you ever found yourself drowning in a sea of your own mail or other documents? Well, it is time to tackle that paper chaos. Don't panic. Kacy Paide, a professional organizer with more than 20 years of experience, has shared tips with Life Kit to make the task less overwhelming.   ✉️ Focus on your closest pile and separate it into active and inactive ones. Active items require follow-up, like calls or bill payments, while inactive items do not.✉️ Clearly mark the due date on active documents with a bold, permanent marker on a sticky note.✉️ Save important documents like birth certificates, passports, product manuals, tax papers and medical records. Choose a method that suits your habits: alphabetize, color-code or simply label. For easy access, place vital documents in a brightly colored folder.✉️ You don't need to shred everything that has your name and address on it. The Federal Trade Commission advises destroying documents containing sensitive information, such as account numbers, birth dates, passwords, signatures and Social Security numbers, to protect against identity theft.✉️ Start small by dedicating just 25 minutes to decluttering. Remember, organizing is an ongoing process that needs regular maintenance and adjustments.   
   Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.   Picture show   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The destroyed location of the original Cafe 11/11 in Kherson, Ukraine.  CREDIT: Svet Jacqueline for NPR UKRAINE
                
                    Svet Jacqueline for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Svet Jacqueline for NPR
    

   
   In Ukraine's Kherson region, a brief ceasefire brought a momentary return to normalcy. Brokered by first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo last week, the truce allowed hundreds of residents to evacuate from a Russian-occupied town and provided a rare few days of peace in a frontline city. Russia and Ukraine agreed to the deal to help Oleshky, a town near Kherson that was occupied by Russian troops in 2022. The troops had mined the land around it, and food and medicine were rarely able to reach the people. This short pause in hostilities was a welcome relief, allowing families to fill the sidewalks, shoppers to hurry to stock up and cafe-goers to enjoy art-filled spaces. These photos capture a brief glimpse of everyday life for these people.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Election cake is a sweet civic tradition dating back to 1771. The annual Election Cake Bake-Off at Connecticut's Old State House in Harford, CT, has continued the celebration for more than 250 years.
                
                    Barbara Glassman Dell
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Barbara Glassman Dell
    

   
   At Connecticut's Old State House, the annual Election Cake Bake-Off has been celebrating the sweet civic tradition of election cake for more than 250 years. This dessert has evolved from what it once was: a tough fruitcake, often soaked in alcohol.Chemical manufacturer 3M has reached a $7.35 billion settlement to resolve thousands of personal injury claims related to toxic chemicals found in firefighting foam. title: Trump's arch is on the verge of federal approval. But a judge could block construction
body:
The government submitted final renderings to the National Capital Planning Commission that depict a 250-foot arch topped with three gold statues and an eternal flame.
                
                    Department of the Interior
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Department of the Interior
    

   
   This could be a make-or-break week for President Trump's triumphal arch.   For months, the Trump administration has barreled toward his dream of building a 250-foot arch in Washington, D.C.: rubber-stamping and side-stepping various federal reviews, cutting out Congress and announcing imminent construction despite a lack of final approval and an ongoing legal battle.   In May, the entirely Trump-appointed Commission for Fine Arts approved the arch's design — still incomplete at the time. In September, a federal council packed with Trump allies abruptly terminated a historic preservation review that participants had already criticized as rushed.   
   It all comes to a head on Thursday, when the National Capital Planning Commission will meet to consider final approval for the controversial structure. The arch is the only item on the agenda; the meeting will be online-only and is expected to take five hours because of the high volume of public participation.   Nearly 120 concerned citizens have signed up to speak, an unusually high number for such meetings and a symbol of the widespread public opposition. Democratic lawmakers, veterans, historic preservationists and more than 100,000 people have spoken out against the arch in written comments, local protests and previous commission meetings.   Among their many concerns, critics say the structure would obstruct an important view, insult service members buried on the hallowed ground of nearby Arlington National Cemetery and add a layer of risk to notoriously complicated D.C. airspace. They see the arch as part of Trump's unilateral effort to memorialize himself in the nation's capital.   The White House has repeatedly said the arch will "enhance the visitor experience at Arlington National Cemetery" and be "one of the most iconic landmarks not only in Washington, D.C., but throughout the world."   
   "It will be one of the great things we've ever done," Trump said from the Reflecting Pool on Monday, giving the arch — alongside several other D.C. construction projects — valuable airtime in his last in-person remarks before the midterm elections.   The planning commission is widely expected to greenlight the arch. It approved preliminary site and building plans over the summer, and its new Trump-appointed chair, Mark Paoletta, expressed his enthusiastic support for the arch in an op-ed published last month. The administration says that after a successful commission vote, all that's needed to break ground is sign-off from its own Department of the Interior.   
   In fact, the government notified a federal judge late last month that, pending those two approvals, "construction could commence as early as" Thursday.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Trump wants to build his arch on the grassy traffic circle on Arlington Memorial Bridge, between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery (the entrance to which is seen in the background). The house on the top of the hill formerly belonged to Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee.
                
                    Saul Loeb/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Saul Loeb/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   It filed that notice as part of the ongoing lawsuit brought by Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian who argue the arch is unlawful without approval from Congress. The Trump administration has not sought that, instead citing Congress' century-old authorization of a pair of columns on that traffic circle that were ultimately never built.   The plaintiffs promptly asked District Judge Tanya Chutkan to issue a preliminary injunction before Thursday's meeting to block the administration from "taking any steps to construct, or to direct or facilitate construction, of any structure in Memorial Circle, absent congressional authorization" while the case plays out.   
   A group of advocacy, historic preservation and conservation organizations quickly signed on to a supporting brief. At a hearing last Friday, Chutkan heard from both sides and expressed skepticism about the government's sense of urgency and national security claims. Then, over the weekend, D.C. and Virginia jointly filed their own lawsuit, calling the arch "flagrantly illegal" for a whole host of reasons.   Chutkan has consolidated the two cases, with all eyes on her docket as Thursday's meeting ticks closer.   On Monday, the judge ordered the government to notify the court within one hour of any arch decision by the National Capital Planning Commission, National Park Service and Department of the Interior — and to provide notice within 30 minutes of "any activity related to or in preparation for the construction of an arch on Memorial Circle."   Chutkan's order suggests she may wait to issue a ruling on construction until after the planning commission meeting, which is scheduled to adjourn at 6 p.m. ET.   On Tuesday, the Trump administration asked Chutkan to clarify and to modify her order to require 24 hours' notice instead, explaining that even though its staff is "working diligently (including nights and weekends) on this matter, it takes time for decisions to be communicated through the various chains and then appropriately drafted into a notice suitable for filing with the Court."   
   The plaintiffs responded with their own filings, opposing that request. They compared the situation to that at D.C.'s East Potomac Park, where the government provided the judge in that case less than a full day's notice before cutting down 430 trees during a holiday weekend.   "Indeed, Defendants recently demonstrated just how much they can change the status quo in a matter of 24 hours," the lawyers wrote.   The judge later clarified her wording but kept the timeline the same.   Hours later, on Wednesday night, the government notified the court that Grunley Construction Company, a Maryland-based firm, "may be — but is not necessarily — arranging off-site preparations for construction mobilization in anticipation of permit approval."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Protesters flocked to Memorial Circle in October to rally against the proposed arch. Several Democratic lawmakers speaking at the event vowed to stop it, or else remove the structure if it does get built.
                
                    Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   How we got here — and what could happen next   The first registered speaker on the meeting agenda is plaintiff Michael Lemmon, the veteran and retired foreign service officer for whom the lawsuit is named. Lemmon has said he hopes to be buried in Arlington National Cemetery one day — but not if there's an arch.   "The thought of being interred in the shadow of what I believe to be a personal vanity project is profoundly disturbing to me," he wrote in a court filing in February, when the case was first filed.   
   The arch would stand 250 feet tall in Memorial Circle, a traffic circle on the bridge that links D.C.'s National Mall to Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia. It would be more than twice the height of the nearby Lincoln Memorial and, by the National Park Service's own admission, disrupt the historical significance of dozens of nearby monuments.   Renderings submitted to the planning commission show a white concrete structure topped with three golden statues, including a winged woman holding a torch with an eternal flame.   That flame was one of the recommendations of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which said in September that the arch would not pose a hazard to airspace as long as it is continuously lit a certain way. Aviation safety experts told NPR that those unconventional lighting recommendations add a new layer of risk — like glare and fire hazards — to an already troubling proposal.   
   Just days after the FAA released its report, Trump announced on social media that the arch would actually serve as a military complex housing snipers and ammunition. Legal experts saw that abrupt rebrand as an attempt to cast the arch as a matter of national security, an argument that has so far helped the administration proceed with its controversial White House ballroom.    The final renderings sent to the planning commission don't mention drones or snipers. But in a seven-page declaration submitted to the court last week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called the arch a "generational national defense opportunity."   On Friday, Chutkan questioned how the government would square installing military equipment with accommodating what it has said could be up to 22,000 civilian visitors per day.   "The arch is somehow supposed to deter assassination attempts on the president?" she said, in response to the government attorney's answers. "It's going to be completed three years from now."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Mark Paoletta, the Trump-appointed chair of the National Capital Planning Commission, pictured at its meeting in October. The commission is tasked with evaluating and approving federal construction projects in D.C.

   As the legal battle over the arch intensifies, one of the Trump administration's primary arguments is that the veterans don't have standing to sue. They point to the Supreme Court's ruling in the ballroom case, though Public Citizen — the group representing the veterans — says the two are very different.   It's in that context that the Democrat-led governments of D.C. and Virginia jumped into the fray with their own lawsuit this weekend. Their 55-page complaint details their grounds for suing as well as the "battery of irreplaceable injuries" they say their communities will suffer "as soon as construction begins — from disruptions of local traffic to environmental degradation to threats to security and emergency preparedness."   The jurisdictions argue that the arch is illegal without congressional authorization and violates federal environmental and historic preservation laws as well as D.C.'s restrictions on building heights.   
   They say an arch would "substantially disrupt daily life in the capital region," including by forcing local governments to divert resources away from other priorities. The lawsuit says an arch at that location would increase traffic and hinder emergency response along one of the main corridors between D.C. and Virginia, complicate the flight path of Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport and threaten local wildlife, all things that governments would have to spend time and resources addressing.   They also have concerns about the construction process itself — from 320-foot cranes disrupting already-complex airspace to excavation work sending sediment into the Potomac River.   
   "These harms cannot be remedied if construction of the Arch proceeds," the complaint reads, adding that "the unlawful construction of a project of this scale will be difficult to undo."   
   The Trump administration has said construction will take two to three years, with crews working 20 hours a day, year-round. It said in a court filing last week that the first six months will involve underground excavation and foundation work, arguing that there is no need for a judge to intervene at this stage because plaintiffs' concerns about the lost view would not be relevant.   But lawyers for D.C. and Virginia say the administration "would suffer no cognizable injury if required to wait before beginning construction of an illegal monument."   "Defendants cannot plausibly claim they have an urgent need to begin building the Arch 101 years after enactment of the statute that they (wrongly) claim authorized its construction and over one year after the President announced his intention to build it," they wrote.   Critics have accused Trump of trying to rush approval of the arch before this week's midterm elections. Democratic lawmakers filed a supporting brief in the suit, with several vowing they will not let the arch proceed if their party retakes control of Congress.

schema.headline: Trump's arch is on the verge of federal approval. But a judge could block construction
